You are also given `change_time` (the cost in seconds to swap to a fresh tire) and `num_laps`, the number of laps to complete. You may switch tires between any laps. Return the minimum total time to finish all num_laps laps.

Example: tires = [[1, 2], [2, 1]], change_time = 3, num_laps = 4. Using the second tire ([2,1], which never slows down) for all 4 laps costs 2+2+2+2 = 8, which beats any plan involving the first tire or a tire change.
hints: A tire is never worth using for more than about 18-20 consecutive laps, since its time grows geometrically; precompute the best single-tire time for every small lap count (1 up to that cap). Then run a DP over the total laps, choosing how many consecutive laps to ride on one tire before paying change_time and starting a fresh stint.

test_cases.explanation: Riding the constant-time tire [2,1] for all 4 laps costs 2+2+2+2=8, the best possible plan.
Riding tire [5,1] for all 3 laps costs 5+5+5=15, which beats changing tires or using the fast-but-degrading tire for long.

title: Maximum Elegance of a K-Length Subsequence
description:
You are given a 2D array `items`, where items[i] = [profit, category]. Choose exactly k items (any subsequence of k of them). The elegance of the chosen set is the sum of their profits, plus the square of the number of distinct categories among them. Return the maximum possible elegance.

Example: items = [[3,2],[5,1],[10,1]], k = 2. Choosing the two highest-profit items, [10,1] and [5,1], gives profit 15 but only 1 distinct category, for elegance 15 + 1 = 16. Swapping [5,1] for [3,2] gives profit 13 with 2 distinct categories, for elegance 13 + 4 = 17, the best possible.
hints: Start with the k highest-profit items as a baseline. Among them, any item that shares its category with an earlier (higher-profit) item is a 'replaceable duplicate' -- swapping the cheapest such duplicate for a later item that introduces a brand-new category can only help, as long as the profit lost is outweighed by the extra category's contribution, so try every such swap in order and keep the best result.

test_cases.explanation: Swapping out the duplicate-category [5,1] for [3,2] trades 2 profit for a new category, raising elegance from 16 to 17.
Every item shares category 1, so no swap can ever add a new category; the best is just the two highest profits, 4 + 2 = 6, plus 1 for a single category: 7.

title: Minimum Number of Visited Cells in a Grid
description:
You are given a 0-indexed m x n grid of non-negative integers. Starting at (0, 0), from any cell (i, j) you may jump to (i, j'), with j < j' <= j + grid[i][j], or to (i', j), with i < i' <= i + grid[i][j] (that is, move right or down by up to grid[i][j] steps, staying in bounds). Return the minimum number of cells visited (including the start and end) to reach (m - 1, n - 1), or -1 if it cannot be reached.

Example: grid = [[3,4,2,1],[4,2,3,1],[2,1,0,0],[2,4,0,0]]. One shortest path visits (0,0), (0,1), (1,3), (3,3), which is 4 cells.
hints: Work backward from the destination. The minimum cells to reach the end from (i, j) is 1 plus the best (smallest) value among every cell reachable in one jump to the right or down from (i, j), which you have already computed since you are filling the grid from the bottom-right corner outward.

test_cases.explanation: A shortest path visits (0,0), (0,1), (1,3) and (3,3), a total of 4 cells.
A shortest path reaches the bottom-right corner in 3 visited cells.

title: Minimum Reverse Operations
description:
There are n positions numbered 0 to n - 1, and a ball currently sits at position `p`. A list `banned` names positions the ball may never land on. In one operation, choose a contiguous window of exactly k positions that contains the ball's current position, and reverse that window; the ball moves to wherever its position lands inside the reversed window (and the move is only allowed if that landing position is not banned). Return an array `ans` of length n, where ans[i] is the minimum number of operations to move the ball to position i (0 for i = p), or -1 if it is unreachable.

Example: n = 4, p = 0, banned = [1, 2], k = 4. The only window of length 4 is the whole array [0,1,2,3]; reversing it moves the ball from 0 to 3 in 1 operation. Positions 1 and 2 are banned and so stay at -1.

A ball at position c, inside a reversed window starting at i of length k, lands at 2i + k - 1 - c.
hints: For a ball at position c, reversing a length-k window [i, i+k-1] that contains c moves it to 2i + k - 1 - c; as the window's start i ranges over its valid choices, the reachable landing spots form a simple arithmetic sequence with step 2. Run a breadth-first search from p, and at each step compute that whole reachable range directly instead of trying every possible window one at a time.

test_cases.explanation: The only length-4 window is the whole array; reversing it sends the ball straight from 0 to 3 in 1 operation.
The only window of length 3 containing position 0 is [0,1,2]; reversing it sends the ball from 0 to 2 in 1 operation, and nothing beyond that is reachable.

title: Minimum Cost to Make Array Equalindromic
description:
You are given an integer array `nums`. In one operation you may change any single element to any integer value, at a cost equal to the absolute difference between the old and new value. The array is equalindromic if every element can be made equal to the same palindromic number. Return the minimum total cost to make nums equalindromic.

Example: nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Turning every element into 3 (itself a palindrome) costs |1-3|+|2-3|+|3-3|+|4-3|+|5-3| = 2+1+0+1+2 = 6, the minimum possible.
hints: The optimal single target value (ignoring the palindrome restriction) is always the median of nums, since that minimizes the sum of absolute differences. Search outward from the median for the nearest palindromic numbers and check the resulting cost for each nearby candidate.

test_cases.explanation: Targeting 3, the median and already a palindrome, costs 2+1+0+1+2=6.
The median is 13, which is not a palindrome; the nearest palindrome is 11, giving cost 1+1+2+3+4=11.

title: Count Increasing Quadruplets
description:
You are given a 0-indexed integer array `nums` of distinct values. Count the quadruplets of indices (i, j, k, l) with i < j < k < l such that nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j] < nums[l] (note the middle two are deliberately out of index order in value: the earlier-indexed one, j, must hold the larger value).

Example: nums = [1, 3, 2, 4, 5]. The quadruplet (0, 1, 2, 3) has values 1, 3, 2, 4, satisfying 1 < 2 < 3 < 4. Checking every quadruplet of indices gives a total of 2 that satisfy the pattern.
constraints: All the integers of nums are unique.
hints: The array is small enough to check every combination of 4 indices directly and test the value pattern on each.

test_cases.explanation: Checking every quadruplet of indices, exactly 2 satisfy nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j] < nums[l].
The values are already fully increasing in index order, so the required out-of-order pattern never happens: 0.

title: Meeting Rooms III
description:
There are n meeting rooms, numbered 0 to n - 1. You are given a 2D array `meetings`, where meetings[i] = [start, end] is the time range a meeting needs. Process the meetings in order of start time: assign a meeting to the lowest-numbered room currently free at its start time; if no room is free, delay the meeting (keeping its original duration) until the earliest moment any room frees up, then assign it to the lowest-numbered room among those that free up at that moment. Return the number of the room that holds the most meetings once all are scheduled, breaking ties by the lowest room number.

Example: n = 2, meetings = [[0,10],[1,5],[2,7],[3,4]]. Room 0 takes [0,10]; room 1 takes [1,5]; [2,7] must wait until room 1 frees at time 5 and runs [5,10] there; [3,4] then waits for whichever room frees first (both free at 10) and, by the tie-break rule, goes to room 0, running [10,11]. Both rooms end up hosting 2 meetings each, and ties go to the lower room number, so the answer is 0.
hints: Keep a min-heap of free room numbers and a min-heap of (end_time, room) for busy rooms. Before handling each meeting, free every room whose end time is at or before the meeting's start. If a room is free, use the lowest-numbered one; otherwise, delay to whichever busy room frees up soonest (ties broken by room number, which the heap handles naturally) and keep the same duration.

test_cases.explanation: Both rooms end up hosting 2 meetings each; the tie goes to the lower room number, 0.
Rooms 1 and 2 both host 2 meetings, tied for the most; the tie goes to the lower room number, 1.

title: Minimum Time to Complete All Tasks
description:
You are given a 2D array `tasks`, where tasks[i] = [start, end, duration] means the i-th task must run for a total of `duration` unit-length time points chosen from the inclusive range [start, end] (the specific points do not need to be contiguous). A computer can only run one task at any single time point, but one time point running can count toward the duration of several tasks whose ranges overlap it. Return the minimum number of time points, across all tasks, that the computer must be running.

Example: tasks = [[2,3,1],[4,5,2],[1,5,2]]. The second task needs 2 points inside [4,5], which forces both 4 and 5 to be chosen; the first task then still needs a point inside [2,3], separate from those two. Running at points {2, 4, 5} covers everything -- the first task gets its point at 2, the second gets both 4 and 5, and the third (needing 2 points in [1,5]) is covered by any two of the three. The minimum is 3 points.
hints: Sort tasks by their end time. For each task, count how many of the already-chosen running points fall in its range; if more are still needed, greedily turn on the latest available points within its range first, since those are more likely to also help later (later-ending) tasks.

test_cases.explanation: The second task forces both 4 and 5 to be chosen, and the first task still needs a separate point in [2,3], giving the minimum set {2, 4, 5}.

title: Minimum Adjacent Swaps for K Consecutive Ones
description:
You are given a binary array `nums` and an integer `k`. In one move you may swap two adjacent elements. Return the minimum number of moves needed to gather some k of the 1s in nums into k consecutive positions.

Example: nums = [1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1], k = 2. The three 1s sit at indices 0, 3 and 5. Swapping to bring the 1s at indices 3 and 5 next to each other takes 1 move; this is the cheapest way to gather any 2 of the 1s.
hints: Record the index of every 1. Subtracting each one's rank among the 1s turns 'gather k consecutive 1s' into 'make k of these transformed values equal', whose minimum-move cost is the sum of absolute differences from their median. Slide a window of k over the transformed positions and take the best.

test_cases.explanation: Gathering the two 1s at indices 3 and 5 together costs just 1 swap, the cheapest option.
All three 1s already span indices 0, 1 and 3; moving the one at index 3 next to the others costs 1 swap.

title: Minimum Number of K Consecutive Bit Flips
description:
You are given a binary array `nums` and an integer `k`. In one move you may choose a contiguous subarray of exactly k elements and flip every bit in it (0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0). Return the minimum number of moves needed to make every element of nums equal to 1, or -1 if it is impossible.

Example: nums = [0, 1, 0], k = 1. Flipping just the first element (a window of size 1) makes it [1, 1, 0], and flipping the last element makes it [1, 1, 1]. Two moves total.
hints: Scan left to right. Whenever the current position (after accounting for the net effect of flips already started) is a 0, you must start a new flip there -- track the running parity of active flips with a difference array instead of actually flipping each window, so each position is processed in constant time.

test_cases.explanation: Flipping the first 0 and then the last 0, each a window of size 1, takes 2 moves in total.
The only 0 is at the last index, but a window of size 2 starting there would run off the end of the array, so no valid flip can ever fix it: the answer is -1.

title: Minimum Number of Days to Disconnect Island
description:
You are given an m x n binary grid representing a map of land (1) and water (0), where the land forms exactly one connected island (connected means sharing an edge, not a corner). Each day, you may turn exactly one land cell into water. The island becomes disconnected once it either splits into two or more separate islands or disappears entirely. Return the minimum number of days needed to disconnect the island.

Example: grid = [[1,1,1]]. Turning the middle cell into water splits the strip into two separate single-cell islands in a single day.
hints: The answer is always 0, 1 or 2: check whether the island is already disconnected (trivially true for an island of at most 1 cell); if not, try removing each land cell one at a time to see whether that alone disconnects it; otherwise the answer is always achievable in exactly 2 days.

test_cases.explanation: Removing the middle cell leaves two isolated single-cell islands, so 1 day suffices.
A solid 2x2 block of land can never be split by removing just one corner, since the remaining three cells stay connected in an L-shape; two removals (opposite corners) are needed.

title: Find the Safest Path in a Grid
description:
You are given an n x n binary matrix `grid` where a 1 marks a cell containing a thief and a 0 marks an empty cell. The safeness factor of a cell is its Manhattan distance to the nearest thief. A path from (0, 0) to (n - 1, n - 1), moving one step up, down, left or right at a time and never landing on a thief, has a safeness factor equal to the minimum safeness factor among all the cells it visits. Return the maximum possible safeness factor over every such path.

Example: grid = [[0,0,1],[0,0,0],[0,0,0]]. Starting and ending cells are both far from the single thief at (0, 2), and a route along the bottom and left edges keeps a distance of at least 2 from it the whole way, for a safeness factor of 2.
constraints: There is at least one thief in the grid.
hints: First run a multi-source breadth-first search from every thief to find each cell's distance to the nearest one. Then find the path that maximizes its minimum safeness, which is a 'widest path' problem: use a max-priority-queue search (like Dijkstra, but maximizing the bottleneck value instead of minimizing a sum) starting from (0,0).

test_cases.explanation: The starting cell (0, 0) is itself a thief's cell, so the safeness factor is forced to 0 no matter which path is taken.
A route hugging the bottom and left edges stays at least 2 steps from the single thief the whole way.

title: Count Stepping Numbers in Range
description:
A stepping number is a positive integer where every pair of adjacent digits differs by exactly 1 (a single-digit number is always a stepping number). Given two integers `low` and `high`, count the stepping numbers in the inclusive range [low, high].

Example: low = 10, high = 20. The stepping numbers in this range are 10 and 12 (1 and 0 differ by 1; 1 and 2 differ by 1), so the answer is 2.
hints: A number is a stepping number exactly when consecutive digits in its decimal representation always differ by exactly 1. For a range this size, checking every integer directly and verifying its digits is fast enough.

test_cases.explanation: 10 and 12 are the only stepping numbers in this range.
Every single-digit number is trivially a stepping number, giving all 9 of them.

title: Maximum Strictly Increasing Cells in a Matrix
description:
You are given an m x n integer matrix `mat`. Starting from any cell, you may repeatedly move to another cell that shares the same row or the same column and has a strictly larger value (the cells do not need to be adjacent). Return the maximum number of cells you can visit this way, including the starting one.

Example: mat = [[3, 1], [3, 4]]. Starting at the 1 (row 0, column 1) and moving down its column to the 4 (row 1, column 1) visits 2 cells; no longer chain exists, since neither 3 shares a row or column with both the 1 and the 4 at once.
hints: Process cells in increasing order of value. Keep the best chain length ending in each row and each column so far; a cell's best chain length is one more than the better of its row's or column's running best. Process all cells of equal value together, using the running bests from strictly before this value, so equal values never chain into each other.

test_cases.explanation: Starting at the 1 and moving down its column to the 4 visits 2 cells; no 3-cell chain exists here.
Every cell holds the same value, so no strictly increasing move is ever possible: the best chain is just 1 cell.

title: Minimum Cost to Convert String I
description:
You are given two equal-length strings `s` and `t`, and three equal-length arrays `original`, `changed` and `cost`. Each index i says: changing a character equal to original[i] into changed[i] costs cost[i] (and this move may be chained with others, possibly through intermediate letters, to reach a cheaper overall cost for the same net change). You may perform any number of these moves, in any order, on any positions of s. Return the minimum total cost to turn s into t, or -1 if it is impossible.

Example: s = "abc", t = "bbd", original = ["a", "b", "c", "c"], changed = ["b", "c", "b", "d"], cost = [2, 5, 5, 1]. Changing the first character from a to b costs 2. The second character is already b. The third character needs c turned into d, which the direct listed edge does at cost 1. Total cost: 2 + 0 + 1 = 3.
constraints: s, t, original and changed consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Build a 26x26 graph where an edge from letter u to letter v has weight equal to the cheapest listed cost for that exact conversion. Run Floyd-Warshall to get the cheapest cost between every pair of letters (allowing multi-step conversions), then sum the cost for each position where s and t differ.

test_cases.explanation: Changing a to b costs 2, b already matches, and changing c directly to d costs 1, for a total of 3.
Each a must go a -> c -> b at cost 1 + 2 = 3, four times, for a total of 12.

title: Stone Game IX
description:
Alice and Bob take turns removing one stone from an array `stones`, with Alice moving first. After a stone is removed, let the running total be the sum of every stone removed so far. If a player's move makes the running total divisible by 3, that player loses immediately (unless it is the very first move's running total that is divisible by 3, which does not count against anyone and play simply continues). If all stones are removed with nobody ever losing by this rule, the game is a draw. Return true if Alice can guarantee a win with optimal play from both sides, and false otherwise.

Example: stones = [2, 1]. Removing either stone first keeps the running total at 2 or 1 (not divisible by 3), and then the only remaining stone makes the total 3, which is divisible by 3 -- whoever removes it second loses, so Alice wins by removing first.
hints: Only the count of stones in each residue class modulo 3 matters, not their exact values. If the count of stones divisible by 3 is even, Alice wins exactly when there is at least one stone in each of the other two residue classes; if it is odd, Alice wins exactly when those two counts differ by more than 2.

test_cases.explanation: With one stone of each non-zero residue and none divisible by 3 (an even count, zero), Alice wins since both residue classes are non-empty.
A single stone whose removal makes the running total 2 (not divisible by 3) leaves nobody else to move, so the game is a draw, not a win for Alice.

title: Maximum Score of a Good Subarray
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. A good subarray is one that includes index k. The score of a subarray is the minimum value in it, multiplied by its length. Return the maximum score over every good subarray.

Example: nums = [1, 4, 3, 7, 4, 5], k = 3. The subarray [4, 3, 7, 4, 5] (indices 1 to 5) includes index 3, has minimum value 3, and length 5, for a score of 15 -- the best achievable.
hints: Start a window at just index k and grow it outward one step at a time, always extending toward whichever neighboring value is larger (that keeps the window's minimum as high as possible for as long as possible). Track the running minimum and the best score seen at every step.

test_cases.explanation: The subarray [4,3,7,4,5] (indices 1 to 5) has minimum 3 and length 5, a score of 15.
Extending to include every 5, 5, 4, 5, 4 keeps a minimum of 4 over a length of 5, a score of 20.

title: Minimum Number of Operations to Make All Array Elements Equal to 1
description:
You are given a positive integer array `nums`. In one operation you may choose two adjacent elements and replace one of them with their greatest common divisor. Return the minimum number of operations needed to make every element of nums equal to 1, or -1 if it is impossible.

Example: nums = [2, 6, 3, 4]. The pair (3, 4) already has gcd 1, so replacing the 4 with gcd(3, 4) = 1 gives [2, 6, 3, 1] in a single operation. Spreading that 1 to the remaining 2, 6 and 3 (one operation each, each time replacing a neighbor with gcd(1, x) = 1) takes 3 more operations, for 4 in total.
hints: If some element is already 1, every other element needs exactly one operation (paired with a neighboring 1, which spreads) to become 1 too. Otherwise, impossible unless the overall gcd of the whole array is 1; in that case, find the shortest subarray whose gcd is 1 (costing length - 1 operations to turn one of its elements into a 1), then spend n - 1 more operations spreading that 1 to everything else.

test_cases.explanation: The pair (3, 4) has gcd 1, so one operation creates a 1, and 3 more operations spread it to the rest: 4 in total.
Every element is even, so the overall gcd can never reach 1: the answer is -1.
